title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
openingText: In a village in La Mancha — the name of which I'd rather not recall — there lived not long ago one of those gentlemen who keep a lance in the rack, an old shield, a lean hack, and a greyhound for hunting. A stew of rather more beef than mutton, a salad most nights, leftovers on Saturdays, lentils on Fridays, and an extra pigeon on Sundays ate up three-quarters of his income. The rest went on a fine wool doublet, velvet breeches with matching shoes for holidays, and his best homespun for weekdays, in which he cut a respectable figure. His household included a housekeeper past forty, a niece under twenty, and a lad who could both saddle the horse and handle the pruning-hook out in the fields and at market. Our gentleman was nearly fifty; he was lean, sinewy, sharp-featured, an early riser and a great hunter. They say his surname was Quixada — or Quesada; the authorities differ — though reasonable inference suggests he was actually called Quexana. This is of little importance to the story; it's enough that the telling not stray a hair's breadth from the truth.
about:
A country gentleman reads so many romances of chivalry that he decides to become a knight himself. Calling himself Don Quixote of La Mancha, he sets out to right wrongs with his old horse Rocinante and, from his second departure, the farmer Sancho Panza as his squire. His ideals can produce courage and generosity, but his mistakes also hurt other people. Sancho questions him, negotiates with him, deceives him and stays with him. Their changing relationship is the thread through a book full of arguments, stories, songs and unexpected encounters.

Cervantes published Part One in 1605 and Part Two in 1615. In the later part, several characters have read the earlier history and use that knowledge to influence the travellers. An unauthorized sequel published under the name Avellaneda also enters the fiction. The novel repeatedly asks who owns a story, whose account deserves belief and what happens when people treat another person as entertainment.

angleCards.title: When a story changes what you see
angleCards.text: Windmills become giants and inns become castles in Don Quixote’s imagination. Watch how the narrator, Sancho and bystanders describe the same encounter, and who bears the cost of a mistake.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare Don Quixote’s interpretation with the other accounts and follow the consequences of his actions.

angleCards.title: Listen to Sancho
angleCards.text: Sancho’s appetite, proverbs and bargaining are more than comic decoration. His practical judgment can outstrip his master’s, but he also wants the rewards his master promises.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how Sancho and Don Quixote influence one another without reducing either to a fixed role.

angleCards.title: Dulcinea as an imagined lady
angleCards.text: Don Quixote gives the name Dulcinea to Aldonza Lorenzo, a woman he remembers from El Toboso. The novel supplies reports, disguises and supposed enchantments rather than a direct meeting with Aldonza that settles the matter.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish what is known about Aldonza from what Don Quixote, Sancho and other characters invent about Dulcinea.

angleCards.title: Who controls the joke?
angleCards.text: Part Two’s hosts sometimes stage events for the travellers. The narrator eventually questions whether the people designing the tricks are any wiser than their victims.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to notice when amusement becomes cruelty and how the book exposes the people arranging it.

cast.name: Don Quixote of La Mancha
cast.description: An older country gentleman who adopts a knightly name and vocation. He can speak thoughtfully on many subjects while interpreting events through chivalric romances. The text gives several variants of his family name before identifying him as Alonso Quixano near the end.

cast.name: Sancho Panza
cast.description: A farmer with a wife, Teresa, and children. He joins the knight with hopes of governing an island. He travels on a donkey called Dapple in this English text and brings shrewdness, self-interest, loyalty and an inexhaustible supply of sayings.

cast.name: Dulcinea del Toboso
cast.role: The lady of the knight’s imagination
cast.description: The ideal Don Quixote builds around Aldonza Lorenzo. Claims that she has appeared or been transformed need to be read in their narrative setting; they do not establish a direct encounter with Aldonza herself.

cast.name: Rocinante
cast.description: A thin, aging horse given a grand new name. His limitations repeatedly collide with his rider’s ambitions. The novel does not narrate his death after his master’s.

cast.name: Cide Hamete Benengeli
cast.description: From Part One, Chapter 9, an Arabic manuscript attributed to this historian becomes the narrator’s supposed source. A translator and editorial comments add further layers between events and readers.

cast.name: Samson Carrasco
cast.description: A university bachelor from Don Quixote’s village who appears in Part Two. His interest in bringing the knight home turns into a series of performances within the story.

whyItMatters.title: A novel about making novels
whyItMatters.body: The book brings together adventure, literary criticism, letters, poems and stories told by its characters. Its competing narrators and its treatment of the rival sequel make the act of storytelling part of the action. Calling it an important foundation of the modern novel is more useful than claiming that it invented every technique it employs.

whyItMatters.title: Comedy with consequences
whyItMatters.body: The characters can be funny and vulnerable at the same time. Beatings, deception, social rank, coercion and exclusion are often uncomfortable parts of the comedy. A character’s judgment is not automatically the narrator’s or the author’s verdict.

whyItMatters.title: Reading this edition
whyItMatters.body: The main text follows 126 chapter divisions: 52 in Part One and 74 in Part Two. Ormsby’s English paragraph divisions are retained, while the modern versions consult the Spanish where the English omits or changes meaning. Chapter 52 also contains the dedication and preface to Part Two. The separate Part One dedication, preface and opening poems belong before Chapter 1. The poems use readable unrhymed modern wording; the opening poems’ deliberately clipped Spanish line endings are explained rather than reproduced.
